h1: Six beer styles for a new brewpub's opening tap list
title: Six Styles for an Opening Tap List | Craft Beer School
desc: A consultant brewer's guide to the six styles a new Indian brewpub should open with: covering every guest, balancing tank time and planning rotation.
teaser: Six taps on opening night. Each one has a job to do. One of them is buying you time.
standfirst: The opening tap list sets the tone for a new brewpub. Choose too narrow and half your guests find nothing they like. Choose too ambitious and your cellar cannot keep up. Here is the six-style list we recommend for most Indian brewpubs and why each one earns its tap.
sections: What an opening list has to do

An opening tap list has three jobs. It must give every guest something to order, from the person who only drinks mainstream lager to the craft enthusiast. It must be brewable in your cellar, with tank times that keep every tap full. And it must show the quality of the brewing from day one, because first impressions travel fast on social media and through office groups.

In consulting work we often see new brewpubs open with too many hop-forward beers, or with a lager that runs out in the first week because nobody planned the tank time. Both are avoidable. Our guide to the first 100 days of a new brewpub covers the wider launch.

1. A light, crisp lager. Helles, pils or a well-made rice lager. This is often your volume leader and the beer that wins over mainstream drinkers. Our guide to Helles explains why it suits most rooms.

2. A wheat beer. Hefeweizen or witbier. Familiar to Indian brewpub regulars, quick to turn in tank and good with food.

3. A pale ale or IPA. The craft drinker's benchmark. A clear, balanced pale ale is easier to keep consistent than a heavily dry hopped hazy IPA in the first months.

4. A dark beer. A stout or porter. It covers guests who want something richer, sells better than many expect even in the heat and pairs well with grilled and roasted food.

5. A light ale or session beer. A blonde ale or Kolsch-style beer for guests who find lager plain and IPA too much.

6. A rotating seasonal. A fruit beer, a spiced beer, a Belgian style or something experimental. This tap keeps regulars coming back and lets the brewer try ideas without risking the core list.

These six styles do not take the same time to brew. A lager typically needs four to six weeks in tank. Most ales need two to three. The wheat beer and the light ale are the fastest. Plan the first month's brew schedule backwards from opening day, so every tap is full when the doors open.

The lager is usually the bottleneck. If it is your biggest seller and your slowest beer, you may need two tanks for it, staggered so one is always ready. Count fermenters against expected sales before you finalise the list, not after.

In the first months your team is still learning the brewhouse. Water, mash efficiency, fermentation behaviour and yeast health all take time to settle. That is why five of the six taps should be steady, repeatable beers. Save the creative work for the seasonal tap.

Write each recipe down with water treatment, mash schedule, fermentation temperatures and dry hop timing. Taste every batch against the last. Fix drift before it reaches the glass.

After a few weeks the sales data will tell you what your guests actually drink. Some brewpubs find the dark beer sells better than expected; others find the IPA needs a lighter sibling. Use the data to adjust the list rather than relying on hunches. Our guide to tap list planning with sales data shows how to read it.

Keep the core steady for at least the first few months. Regulars form habits around their beer. Changing the core too soon loses them.

The opening list is one of the decisions that is hardest to fix later. Tank sizing, brew schedule, recipes and water treatment all depend on it. A second pair of experienced eyes before opening can save weeks of empty taps and inconsistent beer once the doors are open.

Before you lock the list, check four things. Do you have a recent water report and a treatment plan for each style? Can the glycol system hold the lager near freezing while the ales ferment warmer? Have you brewed at least one trial batch of each core beer on the actual kit? Do you have enough yeast, malt and hops in stock for the first two months, given that imported ingredients can take weeks to arrive? If any answer is no, fix it before opening day.
faqs: How many beers should a new brewpub open with?
Six is a practical number for most brewpubs. It covers the main guest types and gives a rotating tap, without overloading the cellar or the brewing team.
Should a brewpub open with a hazy IPA?
It can, but a clear, balanced pale ale is easier to keep consistent while the team learns the brewhouse. Add a hazy IPA once fermentation and dry hopping are reliable.
Which beer usually sells most in an Indian brewpub?
Often the light lager or wheat beer, since many guests start from mainstream lager. Your own sales data after opening is the reliable guide.
